content:
While the claims "Lean is fast", and "Lean is safe & trustworthy" are true, they are still far from being true at the same time: the only officially approved safe proof checking goes through json exports, and no one really trusts native_decide anyway. So I was recently pondering if it would be possible to have an efficient trustworthy proof checker by design.

The dream

  1. The checker is safe and trustworthy. If I have a mathematical challenge, and someone sends me a solution. I can run the checker on the solution, and if the checker says it is verified, it indeed must be. There are no hacks around it -- it cannot hack my computer nor itself.
  2. The checker is fast. More precisely, it can be as fast as any other safe checker up to the constant-(time & memory & disk space) overhead of verifying safety & correctness of the other checker's binary. It could do all the things that high-performance code does, running in parallel, just in time compilation, etc.

Any ideas what would be a good (general but practical) design for this? I expect this question might have been already discussed, if so, I would be happy to look at the appropriate thread.

Have you seen https://github.com/digama0/mm0 ?
Compared to Lean, it does make other trade-offs, in terms of flexibility of syntax, and other UX aspects.

I have heard of MM0, I was not sure if it has the features I am looking for. I need to look into it more deeply, thanks!

In case it does, could it in principle efficiently verify olean files, even with native_decide inside? (once the lean verifier is implemented in MM0-C, or something like that)

I don't know that olean files are a good verification target, but assuming there was some appropriate filetype, as of the last time I worked with mm0 the answer (excluding the native_decide part which is sort of fuzzy) was "yes and no". The mm0 verifier needs to be fed a script of inference steps which would still need to be computed by something that's probably going to look at lot like (and perform a lot like) the lean kernel. That would have certain advantages since it scales better to multiple verifiers and you could probably cache the results of those transformations pretty aggressively (but for a large space cost).

For the two criteria you're presenting, mm0 is generally a closer fit than lean, at least in terms of design/engineering, but as with everything there are trade-offs. You give up a lot of UX elements that people seem to find important, and having a large body of users to actually write a lot of code is important for the "If I have a mathematical challenge, and someone sends me a solution..." part. If the underlying math just doesn't exist in mm0/mm1 yet, then you're SOL, and Lean has significantly more momentum and a much larger community for the time being. Perhaps one day we can benefit from the fruits of an mm0 FRO.

If my understanding is correct, then metamath doesn't exactly seem what I am looking for. My question is not about looking for more efficient set of inference rules but rather how to make arbitrary calculation trustworthy in a principled way with zero overhead (except constant at the initialization). At the same way so that the user only running the proof check does not have to care which software he trusts, and which software he doesn't.

I would not be surprised if there was a principled way of proving an mmc program correct and adding "arbitrary computation" that way, like a verified native_decide (at which point the 'trust' shifts to the spec of the extension, the microcode, the hardware, etc.)
On the Lean side, would it be reasonable to specify what trusting programs represented with Lean.IR.FnBody means? (or did someone already do it?)

May I ask, isn't the entire purpose of Lean to be "safe & trustworthy"? Shouldn't speed then be a secondary metric? And if one can put Lean into a state which optimizes the speed metric, at the cost of safety, then how can one make the statement that Lean is "safe & trustworthy"?

I am genuinely curious, especially with regards to exactly how Lean can be less-than-safe. I understand the user can make a disconnect between the human semantic layer and the machine semantic layer, as explained in the "did I prove it" section where an example is given of a function named "Proof of the Reimann Conjecture" which is not, in fact, such a proof. But if there are examples of logical faults within Lean itself, I am surprised to hear this. Or do I misunderstand the OP?
I believe here the "trustworthy" in "safe & trustworthy" means closer to "logical soundness", and that "safe" means closer to "compiling+running Lean code does not have 'surprising' side effects"
so OP isn't implying that prop_ext quot_ext etc. are unsound

Ok but that said... is the issue that running some kind of speed-up code outside the main kernel can impact on soundness and unintended output (bugs), or is it that the kernel itself can have this behavior within currently allowable use? I'm trying to understand the full limitations of Lean4, is all.

There are a few known examples. A very simple one is

@[implemented_by false] def trueFalse : Bool := true

theorem contradiction : False := by
  have : trueFalse = false := by native_decide
  injection this

and a more sophisticated (by James E Hanson) is

import Mathlib.Data.Nat.Basic
import Mathlib.Tactic
import Mathlib.NumberTheory.FLT.Basic
import Lean

open Lean

unsafe def badNatUnsafe : ℕ := unsafeCast (-4294967296 : ℤ)

@[implemented_by badNatUnsafe] opaque badNatVal : ℕ

run_elab
  addDecl <| .defnDecl {
    name        := .str .anonymous "badNat"
    levelParams := []
    type        := .const ``Nat []
    value       := .lit <| .natVal badNatVal
    hints       := .opaque
    safety      := .safe
  }

theorem FLT : FermatLastTheorem := by
  have truly_marvelous_0 : ¬badNat ≤ 9223372036854775807 := by decide
  have truly_marvelous_1 : ¬9223372036854775807 < badNat := by decide
  simp_all only [not_le]

#print axioms FLT
-- 'FLT' depends on axioms: [propext]

none of these are bugs in the kernel, the first is using generally untrusted native_decide, and the second one is making Lean hack itself in order to get corrupted internal data. The official response to the second one is that if you want to be certain that Lean is not hacking itself (with foreign code), you should use comparator, which essentially exports everything to json, and doesn't trust native_decide.

On the other side of the spectrum, you sometimes need native_decide for verification: bv_decide uses it, interval arithmetics uses it, I used it most recently to verify solutions of puzzle games. I think it is reasonable for start to sacrifice some safety / trustworthiness for speed but as verification progresses, I would like to see people thinking about how to actually close this gap.

And there is also an example of library inconsistency of native_decide even without custom implemented_by.

def foo : Bool := withPtrEq True False (fun () => false) fun eq => nomatch cast eq ⟨⟩
example : foo = false := rfl
#eval foo -- true
example : False := nomatch show foo = true by native_decide

Why even have functions like withPtrEq? Doesn't that just beg for problems? Its bad enough that the statement is clearly ill-typed as written, and that Lean will run with it, but why allow for what looks like essentially memory-hacks instead of keeping the user in the layer above and only allowing kernel access to memory addresses (when directly connected to theorem-level logical statements)?

If anything, this one exposes some interesting issues with the way lean executes code at runtime..

I'm relieved to see, however, that these examples require pretty much malicious intent to execute, and I think I understand now what the OP meant by having a safety-checker. Thank you for taking the time to explain this to me, everyone.

I'm not sure about how to accomplish this in in practice, but I can comment a bit on the theory. One thing you can do (in theory, probably not in practice) is formalize a subset of the x86 specification and then prove theorems of the form "if program A is run on a standard x86 Linux machine and it succeeds with exit code 0, then theorem B is true" (similar style to metamath 0) and then just execute A on your computer. Then you will never actually be able to prove theorem B within Lean, but you can split the checking the proof (which can be checked quickly) and the execution (which can be slow but can take advantage of the x86 processor rather than running within the Lean kernel). You can replace x86 with something like LLVM bytecode or Lean IR but the principle is the same.

Maybe for the sake of concreteness, let's say your goal is to prove that f 100 % 2 = 1 where f 100 is some very expensive computation, and you want to do this via direct evaluation. Your options are

  1. Bypass the Lean elaborator and directly write an expression the Lean kernel will check. This can compute f 100 at whatever speed your kernel can run it at. However, even with a perfect kernel, I think typechecking is just inherently slower than machine code execution.
  2. Do the approach I just outlined where you don't actually prove f 100 % 2 = 1 in Lean but rather prove something like Turing machine M halts implies f 100 % 2 = 1 and then check that M halts empirically.
  3. Add a "reflection principle" to the axiom system of your proof assistant. This would essentially amount to making a robust version of native_decide.

I am having some kind of reflection principle in mind -- I want to run compiled code outside kernel, and still have confidence that I can trust it. I am just not sure

  1. Which representation could be most suitable -- LLVM? Lean.IR? x86? I see this mostly as a practical question.
  2. Would it cover the standard cases that appear in practice: (a) I compile a function once, and then run it on multiple inputs. (b) Someone writes a better (executable) compiler, so after having reasoned about its correctness, I can use it since to compile trusted code instead of using the low-level way of reasoning about code.

Mirek Olšák said:

The official response to the second one is that if you want to be certain that Lean is not hacking itself (with foreign code), you should use comparator, which essentially exports everything to json, and doesn't trust native_decide.

I hope it’s okay to poke at an old thread and note that “using comparator” is now a lot easier with our Comparator Live tool, and James E Hanson’s example is a great demo

Making comparator more user-friendly is nice but doesn't resolve the main speed issue. By the way, I made a prototype of a vibe-coded ITP that could prove that 4244061667345952017 is a prime number by writing a simple checking algorithm (iterating until square root), and verifying it is correct: (by the way, only works on linux x86_64)
